titulo.texto: Siqueiros: From the Porfiriato to the Revolution

frase_gancho.texto: More than seventy-six meters of mural designed to be experienced by walking along it, not from a single spot, and painted with industrial materials.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the next hall, dedicated to Francisco I. Madero, where a fresco by Juan O’Gorman recalls the day the president left this castle on his way to the National Palace.

guion_corto.texto: Can the history of a revolution be painted on a single wall? David Alfaro Siqueiros tried between nineteen fifty-seven and nineteen sixty-six. His mural covers the years from nineteen oh six to nineteen fourteen and is made with acrylic and pyroxylin on cloth-covered wood. It begins with a petrified Porfirio Díaz. It continues with his cabinet trampling the Constitution of eighteen fifty-seven while cancan dancers entertain the powerful. Then it arrives at the Cananea strike and the revolutionary armies. Siqueiros wanted viewers to walk in front of the work, so it is best to take it in slowly, from one end to the other.

guion_largo.texto:
Seventy-six meters eighty-nine centimeters wide: that is the length of this mural, and it cannot be taken in with a single glance. It is four meters forty-six centimeters high. Siqueiros titled it From the Porfiriato to the Revolution and, according to the museum, it covers the years from nineteen oh six to nineteen fourteen. The Guide to Chapultepec Castle, published by the INAH, explains that it is divided into seven sections.

The first section shows a petrified Porfirio Díaz, like a statue that is hardening: a sign that his regime is in decline. In the next one he appears with his cabinet, trampling the Constitution of eighteen fifty-seven. Cancan dancers entertain the aristocrats while the people live in subjugation. Further on comes the Cananea strike of nineteen oh six. Siqueiros considered it the beginning of the revolutionary struggle, and he painted it alongside Karl Marx, Mikhail Bakunin and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. Another section brings together Villistas, Zapatistas and Constitutionalists with their leaders. The last one shows a rider suddenly reining in his horse, and behind him lies a row of the dead: the end of the first stage of the Revolution.

The paradox lies in history itself. Porfirio Díaz had come to power in eighteen seventy-six with a slogan that spoke of free suffrage, no reelection and respect for the Constitution of eighteen fifty-seven. Afterward he was reelected again and again, until nineteen ten. Meanwhile, the country exported henequen, chicle, coffee, rubber and metals, and displayed pavilions at the world’s fairs in Philadelphia, New Orleans and Paris. At the same time, the Maya, the Yaqui and the Mayo were put down with fire and blood. In nineteen oh eight, Díaz told the American journalist James Creelman that he would not seek another term. He did not keep his word: in May of nineteen eleven he went into exile from Veracruz, aboard the German steamship Ypiranga.

In the Cananea scene, the national flag is contested with the head of the mining company. Accounts do not agree on the name of the miner portrayed, so it is best to see him as a symbol of the conflict between workers and the company.

Siqueiros had spent decades searching for modern materials and tools. He experimented with silicone, vinylite, pyroxylin and acrylic, and did research in a workshop at the National Polytechnic Institute. He used tools such as the spray gun and the airbrush. He also championed polyangularity. It was a way of composing that replaced the fixed perspective of the Renaissance with a dynamic space made of walls, ceilings and floors. He wanted the viewer to stop being passive. A phrase attributed to him sums up the idea: a mural must make the viewer walk. This long wall is best understood that way, in motion.

The mural did not move forward smoothly. On the ninth of August, nineteen sixty, Siqueiros was arrested and taken to Lecumberri prison. He was accused of social dissolution, a political crime of that era. He was imprisoned for almost four years. In prison he was allowed to paint, he made stage sets for the prison theater, and he produced more than two hundred works. On the thirteenth of July, nineteen sixty-four, he was released through a presidential pardon that cited his important services to the Nation. He resumed the mural and finished it in nineteen sixty-six.

Lecumberri is the same prison where they took [Francisco I. Madero](chap_10_mural_madero) the night he was murdered, in nineteen thirteen. Today the building houses the General Archive of the Nation.

It is worth viewing this work with one clear idea in mind: it is an interpretation of history made by an artist with a definite political stance, not a neutral document. The museum also preserves personal objects belonging to Porfirio Díaz and his wife, Carmen Romero Rubio. Further on you will be able to discover that other side in the [bedroom of Porfirio and Carmen](chap_21_recamara_porfirio_carmen). Comparing the painted image with everyday life helps us understand a complex era.

texto.Author: David Alfaro Siqueiros
texto.Technique: Acrylic and pyroxylin on cloth-covered wood
texto.Subject: From 1906 to 1914, from the twilight of the Porfiriato to the end of the first stage of the Revolution

texto.pregunta: Myth: All the murals in the Castle are painted in fresco, with lime and pigment on the wall.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The Siqueiros is acrylic and pyroxylin on cloth-covered wood, and the one by González Camarena is also acrylic on cloth-covered wood. Fresco was used by other artists in the museum, such as Juan O’Gorman.
